newsitem.title: HONG KONG: London to keep close eye on HK freedoms after 1997.
newsitem.headline: London to keep close eye on HK freedoms after 1997.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Friday London would keep a close watch on Hong Kong to ensure its rights and freedoms are preserved after the territory returns to Chinese rule.
Clarke, speaking at a conference of Hong Kong's monetary authority and the International Monetary Fund, said Hong Kong's freedoms and rights underpinned its economic success.
Hong Kong, a British colony of more than 150 years, will return to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30.

Under a 1984 Sino-British treaty on Hong Kong's handover known as the Joint Declaration, the territory is guaranteed a high degree of self-rule and the retention of its capitalist system for 50 years after the handover.
"Britain will continue to contribute substantially to Hong Kong's economic success," Clarke said.

"As a signatory of the Joint Declaration, we will continue to take a close interest in ensuring that Hong Kong's economic achievements, and the rights and freedoms which underpin them are fully preserved," he said.
Clarke also said a transparent rule of law and sensible economic policies, as practised under British rule, should be continued in Hong Kong after the sovereignty change.

"Hong Kong's continued success must be built upon the continuation of sensible economic and financial policies, supported by a clear and transparent system of law and administration that has ensured success under British rule and which lie at the heart of the Joint Declaration," he said.
China's plan to scrap Hong Kong's existing elected Legislative Council and install an appointed provisional body has been opposed by Britain and the United States.

Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen said on Friday that British opposition to China's plans to disband the colony's legislature was unreasonable but would not affect the smooth transfer of power this year.
Beijing has also said it plans to roll back the territory's laws on civil liberties, a move that provoked a fierce outcry among pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong and sparked international concern.
